--- execute: warning: false knitr: opts_knit: global.par: true opts_chunk: comment: '' --- # Pipes {#sec-pipes} ## Introduction :::{.callout-note} In its basic form, a pipe allows writing: `f(x)` as `x |> f()` and, similarly, `g(f(x))` as `x |> f() |> g()`. ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Illustration of pipes in R.](assets/R_pipes.webp){#fig-pipe fig-align='center' width=80%} ::: ::: A pipe operator was first introduced to R by the [magrittr](https://magrittr.tidyverse.org/) package with the `%>%` symbol. Note that a number of other packages that endorse the use of pipes export the pipe operator as well. Starting with R version 4.1 (May 2021), a native pipe operator is included with the `|>` symbol. A pipe allows writing `f(x)` as `x |> f()` (native pipe) or `x %>% f` (magrittr). Note that the native pipe requires parentheses, but magrittr works with or without them. A pipe is often used to: - avoid multiple temporary assignments in a multistep procedure, or - as an alternative to nesting functions. Some packages and developers promote its use, others discourage it. You should try and see if/when it suits your needs. The following: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} x <- f1(x) x <- f2(x) x <- f3(x) ``` ::: is equivalent to: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} x <- f3(f2(f1(x))) ``` ::: is equivalent to: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} x <- x |> f1() |> f2() |> f3() ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} iris[, -5] |> split(iris$Species) |> lapply(function(i) sapply(i, mean)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` $setosa Sepal.Length Sepal.Width Petal.Length Petal.Width 5.006 3.428 1.462 0.246 $versicolor Sepal.Length Sepal.Width Petal.Length Petal.Width 5.936 2.770 4.260 1.326 $virginica Sepal.Length Sepal.Width Petal.Length Petal.Width 6.588 2.974 5.552 2.026 ``` ::: ::: Pipes are used extensively in the [tidyverse](https://www.tidyverse.org) packages and many other third-party packages. You can learn more about the magrittr pipe operator in the [vignette](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/magrittr/vignettes/magrittr.html). ::: callout-tip In [RStudio](https://posit.co/products/open-source/rstudio/) the keyboard shortcut for the pipe operator is `Shift-Command-M` (MacOS) or `Ctrl-Shift-M` (Windows). ::: ## Differences between native pipe and **magrittr** Native pipe requires parenthesis (`()`) after function name, **magrittr** works with or without them. For example, ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} x <- rnorm(300) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} x |> mean() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] -0.09332717 ``` ::: ::: but this would fail: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} x |> mean ``` ::: while either works in **magrittr**: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(magrittr) x %>% mean() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] -0.09332717 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} x %>% mean ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] -0.09332717 ``` ::: ::: The native pipe passes its LHS to the first ***unnamed*** argument on the RHS. Alternatively, it can be passed to any named argument using an underscore ("_") symbol. On the other hand, **magrittr** allows using a period `.` to pipe to any position on the RHS. The native pipe workaround is using an anonymous function (can use the new shorter syntax `\(x)` instead of `function(x)`).

Example: Find the position of "r" in the latin alphabet Here, we want to pass the LHS to the second argument of `grep()`. Using native pipe, we name the first argument `pattern` and the LHS is passed to the first unnamed argument, i.e. the second (which is `x`, the character vector where matches are looked for): Native pipe or magrittr: pass to the first unnamed argument: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} letters |> grep(pattern = "r") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 18 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} letters %>% grep(pattern = "r") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 18 ``` ::: ::: Native pipe: pass to any named argument using an underscore (`_`) placeholder, but argument must be named: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} letters |> grep("r", x = _) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 18 ``` ::: ::: **magrittr**: pass to any argument using a period (`.`) placeholder. Argument can be named or not (i.e. positional): ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} letters %>% grep("r", x = .) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 18 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} letters %>% grep("r", .) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 18 ``` ::: ::: For demonstration purposes, here's how you can achieve the same using the native pipe and an anonymous function. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # positional: letters |> {\(x) grep("r", x)}() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 18 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} # named: letters |> {\(x) grep("r", x=x)}() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 18 ``` ::: :::
